The common coral trout, Plectropomus leopardus, is a large-bodied serranid that inhabits coral reef ecosystems throughout the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that this species attains an ultimate total length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters], a size that places it among the larger epinephelines on the Great Barrier Reef. The relationship between total length and body mass in this species follows a power-law function, and from this allometric equation, the predicted ultimate wet weight is approximately 25,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 25,200 grams] for individuals reaching that maximum length. This substantial adult mass reflects the species' position as a top predator within its reef habitat. Young-of-the-year individuals, by contrast, begin life at an exceedingly small size, with hatchlings emerging from pelagic eggs that measure roughly 0.8 millimeters in diameter. Based on the geometric volume of such an egg, the estimated wet weight at birth is 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value that underscores the drastic ontogenetic increase in biomass that must occur over the course of the fish's development to adulthood. This initial mass is notably lower than that reported for many other predatory teleosts of comparable ultimate size.

Sexual maturation in Plectropomus leopardus occurs at a body size considerably smaller than the species' asymptotic length, a pattern common among iteroparous reef fishes that begin reproducing well before somatic growth ceases. Detailed histological examination of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across the species' range has established that the standard length at puberty is 37.3 centimeters [Lp = 37.3 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, derived from the same length-weight relationship used for the ultimate mass calculation, is 721 grams [Wwp = 721 grams]. This body mass at the onset of sexual maturity, 721 grams, is substantially larger than that observed in many co-occurring serranids of similar length, likely reflecting the species' predatory lifestyle and high somatic investment prior to reproductive allocation. The onset of reproductive activity is also strongly influenced by environmental temperature, with spawning events in wild populations occurring during the austral summer when water temperatures are elevated, although the thermal conditions during early development play a critical role in determining the pace of maturation.

Embryonic development and the transition to exogenous feeding are tightly coupled to incubation temperature in this species. Incubation experiments conducted at a stable 28 °C [T = 28 °C] reveal that yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after 8 days [ab = 8 days], a hatching interval that aligns with the rapid developmental rates typical of tropical serranids and is considerably shorter than the incubation periods observed in temperate congeners that develop at cooler temperatures. The newly emerged prolarvae measure only a few millimeters and rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the initial days post-hatching. The temperature used in these incubation experiments, 28 °C, approximates the average summer sea surface temperature across much of the species' core distribution on the Great Barrier Reef, suggesting that the developmental timeline observed in the lab closely mirrors natural hatching schedules in the wild.

The longevity of Plectropomus leopardus has been estimated from otolith-based age validation studies, which indicate that individuals can survive for multiple decades under natural conditions. The maximum lifespan for this species, recorded at a thermal regime of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], is 26 years [am = 26 years]. This figure represents the oldest documented individual observed in mark-recapture programs and is consistent with the extended lifespans reported for other large predatory serranids that occupy stable coral reef environments. The thermal regime during early development, at 28 °C, not only dictates hatching schedules but has been linked to metabolic scaling throughout life, with warmer temperatures accelerating both growth and senescence in this long-lived serranid. Such longevity, when coupled with the relatively late attainment of sexual maturity, means that a typical individual may spend only a portion of its total lifespan in a reproductively active state, a life-history strategy that renders the species vulnerable to overfishing of mature individuals.

Reproductive output in the common coral trout has been quantified through volumetric analysis of ovarian tissue from gravid females captured during the peak spawning season. The maximum reproduction rate, measured under conditions where ambient water temperature reached 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C], is derived from the total fecundity per spawning season. Females produce an estimated 457,900 eggs per spawning season [Ri = 457,900 eggs per spawning season] and exhibit roughly 1.0 spawning events per year [F_R_i = roughly 1.0 spawning events per year], yielding a daily average that reflects the protracted nature of the spawning period. The relatively cool temperature of 17.2 °C [T = 17.2 °C] at which these measurements were taken is notably lower than the typical summer spawning temperatures for this tropical species, and it remains unclear whether this represents a transient upwelling effect or a record from the southern edge of the species' distribution, where such thermal conditions may occur during the early spring.
